opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The mental model I keep coming back to is the gap between capability and reliability. If you look at any individual step, whether that's running a command, reading the output, or deciding what to do next, today's models are often quite good. They can write a reasonable shell command, they know the flags, and they can interpret most error messages. So if you just ask "can the model do this step?" the answer is frequently yes.

But long sequences of commands don't fail because of any one step. They fail because errors compound. If you're 95% reliable per step and you need to chain fifty steps together, the math is brutal. And it's worse than simple multiplication, because the errors aren't independent. An agent misreads one output, forms a slightly wrong belief about the state of the system, and every later action builds on that wrong belief. It doesn't just make one mistake. It goes off the rails in a confident, coherent-looking way.

So I find it useful to ask two separate questions. First, can the agent ever do the task? That's capability, and it's what most benchmarks measure, often as pass@k or best-case performance. Second, does it do the task every time, and does it fail gracefully when it doesn't? That's reliability, and it's what matters if you're actually going to let it touch your systems. Those two curves are improving at very different rates. Capability has jumped dramatically. Reliability on long-horizon tasks has improved too, but much more slowly.

The second part of my mental model is about the environment. The shell is unforgiving. Commands have side effects, some are irreversible, and the feedback is often ambiguous. A command that silently succeeds at the wrong thing looks the same as one that did the right thing. Humans handle this with a lot of tacit knowledge: sanity checks, a sense of when something smells off, knowing when to stop and ask. Agents are getting better at self-verification, but that's where much of the remaining gap is.

Practically, this means I'm skeptical of headline benchmark numbers being read as "agents can now do X job." I'd rather see consistency across repeated runs, cost, and how often a human has to intervene. And for deployment, the sensible approach right now is to design around the reliability gap: sandboxing, checkpoints, reversible actions, and humans in the loop at the points where mistakes are costly. That's not a knock on the technology. It's just how we've always adopted powerful but imperfect tools.

r002.rationale: It says agents can build on an incorrect belief about system state, but does not identify tracking evolving filesystem state as the specific difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
The mental model I find most useful is to think of it as a reliability problem rather than a capability problem. If you look at any single step in a long sequence of shell commands, today's agents are usually quite good. They know the syntax, they know the common tools, they can read error output and make sensible guesses about what went wrong. The hard part is that a task with thirty or forty steps is really a product of all those per-step success probabilities, and that product falls off fast. Even if you're at 98 percent per step, which sounds impressive, you're somewhere around 50 percent on a forty-step task. So you end up with this gap between how good the agent looks in a demo, where each individual action seems smart, and how often it actually finishes the job.

The second piece of the model is that errors aren't independent. In the real world, a mistake in step five doesn't just cost you step five. It changes the state of the system, and now every subsequent step is operating on a world the agent misunderstands. The agent might delete a file, or cd into the wrong directory, or install a slightly wrong version of a dependency, and then confidently proceed as if everything is fine. So the failure mode you see most often is not the agent throwing up its hands. It's the agent drifting, building an increasingly wrong picture of the environment while still producing plausible-looking commands. That's why I'd argue the key capability isn't knowing more shell commands, it's recognizing when you've lost the thread and need to verify your assumptions, and that kind of self-monitoring is still fairly immature.

The third piece, and this is the one I think gets neglected, is that the environment does a lot of the work. If you give an agent good tooling, meaning fast feedback, idempotent operations, the ability to roll back, clear error messages, it looks dramatically more capable. If you drop it into a messy legacy system where commands fail silently or have side effects you can't observe, it looks much worse. So when people ask me how good agents are at this, my honest answer is that it depends almost as much on how the task is scaffolded as on the model. A lot of what gets reported as progress in agent capability is really progress in the harness around the model, and I think it's worth being clear-eyed about that distinction when we try to reason about where things are headed.

r001.rationale: The response attributes difficulty to compounding step failures, error propagation, and environment scaffolding; it does not suggest web interactions poorly represent extended shell workflows.

r002.rationale: It contrasts agents’ competence at individual steps with long tasks and explains that mistakes change system state, such as deleting files or entering the wrong directory, which later steps may misunderstand.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention rock-paper-scissors or failing to recognize that revealing a move first allows a winning counter-move.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a reliability problem that compounds over time. An agent might be very good at choosing the next shell command, but completing a task requires a whole sequence of decisions to work out. If each step has a 95 percent chance of being correct, and you need twenty correct steps, the probability of getting through all of them is only about 36 percent.

Of course, that’s a simplified model. Errors aren’t independent, and a wrong command doesn’t necessarily mean the task is over. The agent can inspect the output, recognize a mistake, and recover. So the important question is whether it can keep track of what it’s trying to accomplish, verify that it’s making progress, and change course when something goes wrong. Being good at individual commands is one capability; reliably managing that whole process is another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a reliability problem that compounds over time. An agent might be very good at choosing the next shell command, but completing a task can require dozens of commands, each depending on what happened before. Even a small chance of making a consequential mistake at each step can translate into a substantial chance of failing the overall task.

Now, that’s only a starting point, because mistakes aren’t necessarily independent, and agents can recover. So the more useful question is: Can the agent tell when it’s gone off track? Can it inspect the result, revise its understanding, and get back to a good state? That feedback loop matters much more than whether it can generate a plausible command. A long sequence of individually reasonable actions doesn’t necessarily add up to a successfully completed task.
